children: White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett said the Trump administration would support the Federal Reserve’s coming interest-rate decision, even as he argued that recent inflation data does not justify another increase.
Speaking Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union,” the National Economic Council director also said administration officials are preparing to discuss possible artificial-intelligence safeguards following
from Anthropic
CEO Dario Amodei.
Fed decision looms
Hassett said President Donald Trump “100% respects the independence” of Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and would accept whatever the central bank decides this week.

Still, Hassett said he and Trump believe rates should not rise. He pointed to a slowdown in inflation during the past three months, arguing that recent data provide a more encouraging picture than the 12-month figures.

The consumer price index rose 3.4% in August from a year earlier and 0.4% from July. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased 2.4% over the year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Hassett attributed some of the earlier inflation pressure to surging oil prices during the conflict in the Persian Gulf. He also argued that the Fed historically has been reluctant to change rates shortly before an election because it wants to protect its political independence.

For investors, the remarks offer reassurance that the White House does not plan to challenge an unfavorable Fed decision immediately. However, Trump’s continued public pressure for lower rates could keep questions about central-bank independence hanging over bonds, currencies and rate-sensitive stocks.
Trump trade threat played down
Hassett also softened Trump’s threat to halt trade with countries that run surpluses with the United States if the Fed does not lower rates.
“I don’t expect trade’s going to go to zero,” Hassett said, characterizing the president’s comments primarily as an expression of his strong preference for lower borrowing costs.

A sweeping suspension of trade with countries including China, Canada, Mexico, Germany and Japan would disrupt supply chains and likely raise prices for American consumers and businesses. Hassett’s response suggested the administration is unlikely to carry out the threat literally.
White House considers AI oversight
On artificial intelligence, Hassett rejected the suggestion that warnings from technology executives would necessarily cause market turmoil.
He described Amodei’s recent proposal as thoughtful and said the administration would study its recommendations. The Anthropic

chief has urged developers to slow the introduction of more powerful systems long enough for safety measures to catch up. He also proposed giving independent evaluators greater access to AI companies’ development work. Other industry leaders have expressed support for stronger safety measures.

Hassett said White House technology and cybersecurity officials are expected to meet this week to consider possible guardrails. Trump has said he is open to some protections while warning that excessive restrictions could weaken the United States in its competition with China. Reuters reported that Trump continues to emphasize maintaining U.S. leadership in advanced AI.
Hassett said the government must address the risk of AI agents carrying out cyberattacks while avoiding a slowdown that allows hostile countries or organizations to develop superior systems.

“The far bigger risk is that a malevolent actor has access to an AI that’s better than the one we have that can protect us,” he said, citing the potential use of advanced models to develop biological weapons.

For technology investors, the emerging policy discussion presents a two-sided risk. Independent monitoring and new safety standards could raise compliance costs for AI developers, but a measured federal framework could also reduce uncertainty and strengthen public confidence in the industry.

title: Hassett says White House will respect Fed decision, weighs AI safety guardrails
